title: Bangladesh Measles Death Toll Reaches 1,205 in World's Worst Outbreak This Year
excerpt: Bangladesh has recorded 216,765 suspected measles cases since March, with children under five accounting for 94% of deaths, after vaccination coverage fell below the 95% herd-immunity threshold in 2025.
body:
• Bangladesh's measles death toll reached 1,205 on October 21 — 104 laboratory-confirmed deaths and 1,101 suspected — with 216,765 suspected cases and 23,212 confirmed infections since March 15, according to the DGHS.
  • Children under five account for 94% of reported deaths, the WHO said, in what it describes through reported figures as the world's worst measles outbreak this year.
  • Vaccination coverage fell below the 95% herd-immunity threshold in 2025: first-dose coverage dropped to 90% from 96% in 2024, and second-dose coverage to 86% from 93%.
  • For families travelling to the region, the WHO advises checking measles vaccination status — two doses protect up to 97% — and catching up missed doses before travel; see the WHO measles page.

Bangladesh's measles outbreak has killed 1,205 people, most of them young children, and health officials are still recording close to a thousand new suspected cases a day. One more child died in the 24 hours to 8am on October 21, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), taking the combined toll of suspected and laboratory-confirmed measles-related deaths to 1,205.

The Latest Numbers

The DGHS recorded 997 new suspected cases in the latest 24-hour period, taking cumulative suspected cases nationwide to 216,765, and 13 new laboratory-confirmed cases, bringing confirmed infections to 23,212, according to The Business Standard. Since March 15, 192,695 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised and 185,110 have recovered. Of the 1,205 deaths, 104 were confirmed through laboratory tests and 1,101 were classified as suspected measles-related deaths.

https://x.com/airnewsalerts/status/2112914332036235562

The World Health Organization has reported that Bangladesh recorded more suspected measles cases than any other country this year — 202,000 suspected cases, 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed, between mid-March and October 9 — with children under five accounting for 94% of reported deaths at that stage.

How Coverage Collapsed

Bangladesh was until recently a vaccination success story. WHO and UNICEF estimates put first-dose measles coverage at 96% in 2024 and second-dose coverage at 93%. In 2025, after political turmoil that followed the 2024 protests ending Sheikh Hasina's rule, health workers struck, vaccine orders were delayed and routine programmes were disrupted. Estimated coverage fell to 90% for the first dose and 86% for the second — both below the 95% level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. A Reuters investigation based on WHO documents and interviews with scientists, health workers and officials found the response was also hampered by data that left out millions of children, weak preparation and failure to reach enough parents, according to Reuters.

"This is a real warning to every country. The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died."

— Mark Jit, WHO vaccine adviser and professor at New York University

The Response

Bangladesh's health ministry says it has immunised more than 20 million children through special campaigns since April, on top of routine vaccination, and at the end of September the government launched a campaign targeting 3.4 million children who had previously been missed. Health experts are also calling for wider vaccination among children older than five, who account for around a third of cases, according to the WHO.

What It Means for Readers

Measles is among the most contagious diseases known, and the WHO notes on its measles health topic page that vaccination remains the best protection. Families in the diaspora planning travel to Bangladesh or elsewhere in South Asia should confirm that children have received both measles-containing doses and arrange catch-up vaccination before travel if doses were missed. The outbreak's lesson travels further than Bangladesh: where coverage slips even a few points below 95%, the virus finds the gap.
